The Superintendent Who Turned Around A School District

Started off wanting to like this lady. I'm a big supporter of education. By the end I wanted to strangle her. All her "turn around" results are predicated upon increased standardized testing scores. These do FUCKING NOTHING for students long term. She's just taught teachers to teach to the test better. Another point of rage was for placing "many teachers in poverty for a week in a simulation." Teachers aren't exactly balling out of control to begin with.

Education starts with the HOME not with the government. There are a million FREE resources out there for kids to leverage ranging from libraries to Khan Academy, etc. The parents need to be educated on how to raise their kids correctly, not how to shift all responsibility to the tax payers.

I've been working in education consulting for about 14 years, especially in the area of test prep, and I can tell you that you shouldn't believe pretty much anything you read about standardized tests, because almost everything depends on whether you're teaching to a good test or a bad one. The ACT and SAT (at least the version that goes away this month) are pretty fucking good tests, and that's why you'll see at the end of the article that only 36% of her graduates are college/career ready.

State-level, No-Child-Left-Behind style tests vary wildly. Connecticut's CAPT is a pretty good test, last time I checked, while New York's Regents is pretty shit. I think that has something to do with the CAPT being instituted in 1995, seven years before NCLB, done Connecticut style by Connecticut educators and the Connecticut Board of Ed. As far as I can tell, New York... got told by the feds to institute tests, and said, "Oh shit, how are we going to get the South Bronx out of high school?" I don't know shit about Missouri's tests, especially cuz NCLB is over now, right? Maybe they're OK, maybe not. I'm guessing less than awesome if they're turning up different results from the SAT/ACT, though.

Khan Academy is pretty good, yeah, but he's still a hedge fund guy, and it shows sometimes. For example, I found an error in his video comparing the old and new SATs. Not a huge deal, a rookie mistake, really, but potentially disastrous for a kid growing up in ass-fuck who doesn't know shit and doesn't have any real teachers/tutors/counselors paying close attention to them.

You're right, parenting is fucking huge. A linguistics study that was ignored because it was the University of Kansas and they conflicted with Noam Chomsky, has proven to be correct, and Chomsky wrong. The neural structures for vocabulary acquisition are almost all wired up in the first 36 months of life. (Or something similar. Memory might be off a touch on that.) Parents do need to be educated, which is what the Harlem Children's Zone model is all about. It's just easier said than done. Also, Roland G. Fryer's analysis of the data in HCZ has indicated that community programs (Head Start, parental education, etc.) are not enough. True elimination of the race gap only occurs when a kid has both community programs AND charter schools.

And you're right, Americans spend more on education than they do on anything except health care, including more than defense. That said, if you look at New York, which is usually the biggest spender, the expenditure per kid per annum in Scarsdale is roughly 150% of the state average, so you know the South Bronx isn't running through the same amount of money.

This lady is in a poor district in Missouri, so I can't imagine she's got TONS of taxpayer dollars--education is usually funded by property taxes, remember--but she IS spending what she has intelligently. The kids do actually need food and health care far more than they need administrative bloat.

Finally, pretty much nobody but bankers are balling out of control these days, but teachers are by definition educated, and while a few do come up from the hood and return to teach in it, they are by far the exception. Point is, there is usually a gap in background and childhood experience that can present a blind spot, especially for new teachers, which can impair educational outcomes. All effective teaching is the integration of new and unknown information into old and known information. If you as a teacher do not understand what your students already know, you will be unable to construct the next layer of understanding in your students' minds. Also, I think liberal NPR is using race dog whistles here as fluently as Mitt Romney and the like, and by "poverty", they probably mean poor and black. A newly-minted poor white teacher who grew up in a community with mostly intact families and resident fathers or even step-fathers could conceivably benefit greatly from a week-long simulation program--and then not quit after one year out of feeling ineffectual. It could also be a profoundly useless and shitty exercise. More likely, it's a mixed bag of good points and bad points.

This is a massively complex topic, and this article oversimplifies a truckload of important points. I would just suggest that other articles you may have read may also have made significant oversimplifications.
